narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 55.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. While the average student who was accepted ranked around the 6th decile, you placed in the 3rd decile, signaling noticeably weaker performance in that critical later period.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction and was the second most important factor. At 37, it sits almost exactly at the average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction slightly toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.90 was the third most influential element; it fell below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants and gently nudged the outcome back toward failure.

Taken together, the model saw your lower third-year ranking and undergraduate grades as outweighing the neutral effect of your LSAT, resulting in an overall forecast that you were more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on strengthening the areas that hurt your profile. Retake challenging courses if possible, seek out intensive bar-prep support early, and consider reapplying once you have demonstrably improved your academic standing or gained relevant professional experience that can offset the earlier record.
